_what_this_is: Everything a pad or a keyboard can say, and nothing about what any of it
That split is this package's own rule -- it reports that the left stick is at
(0.4, -0.9), that A is down and that keypad_8 is down, and deciding that any
of that is 0.2 m/s forward belongs to whoever is driving. So the words live
here and the meanings live with the consumer: `[[fsm.button]]` in a deploy
Read by three programs and written by none of them:
deploy/fsm/src/vocabulary.rs    include_str!, so a board carries no file
It had a copy in each of those for a day. Adding a word meant remembering two
other files, and forgetting one leaves a name that reads as supported and is
refused on build -- or, worse, the other way round.
Was `kk-gamepad-vocabulary/1`, when the pad was the only thing it described.
The keys below were a closed list too and were not written down anywhere a
consumer could check, so `[[fsm.button]] key = ...` took any string at all: a
typo loaded, bound nothing, and looked exactly like a rule that had not fired.

_source.note: It normalises three different pads onto these names, so they mean the same thing on a bench and on the robot. Its own docs put the count at 18: 10 buttons + 2 dpad axes + 6 axes.

buttons.name: X
buttons.unresolved: controller/xbox.py reads evdev 307 as `y` and 308 as `x`; the service's table reads 307 as X and 308 as Y. One is wrong about which physical button it is and pressing it is the only way to find out which.

buttons.name: home
buttons.note: `xbox` in controller/xbox.py. Same button, two names.

_dpad_note: The wire carries dpad_x / dpad_y as -1 / 0 / +1, which no gesture can read, so they are offered as four booleans. The service negates dpad_y so +1 is up; it does not negate Ly, two lines away in the same function.

axes.name: Ly
axes.note: Not negated by the service. Forward is the negative end, by evdev's convention -- stated in controller/xbox.py and never measured against this service.

axes.name: LT
axes.note: Unipolar: a trigger never reports negative.

_axes_note: Sticks carry a 0.15 deadband that is already applied **and rescaled**, so full deflection still reaches ±1. A consumer that applies its own on top narrows what a person can ask for and cannot see that it has.
_modifiers_note: A modifier is either of its two keys: `ctrl` is down while the left Ctrl or the
right one is. A keyboard binding may name one on its own -- `ctrl`, a key like
any other -- or in front of a key, `shift+key_j`, which is J while Shift is
held. A key bound both ways answers the modified binding while its modifier is
down and the plain one otherwise, so J and Shift + J are two things and never
both. A mode switch names one as `with`, as a pad switch names `menu`.
Alt costs a browser something: pressed and let go on its own, Windows moves
focus to the browser's menu, and the keys after it go there rather than to the
page, which has to `preventDefault` it. MuJoCo's viewer uses all three with the
mouse and does nothing with any of them alone.
_keys_note: The numeric keypad, and letters as a task asks for them -- each one knowing
what it costs.
The keypad is the set MuJoCo's viewer does not bind. Everything else on the
main keyboard is bound: `Simulate` handles its shortcuts in C++ and calls the
user callback **as well as**, never instead, so a letter fires both actions
and there is no way to intercept the second.
MEASURED against this repository's mujoco, by reading `mjVISSTRING` and
`mjRNDSTRING` -- **all twenty-six letters are taken**, one render flag each:
A auto-connect  B perturb force  C contact point  D static body
E equality      F contact force  G fog            H convex hull
I inertia       J joint          K skybox         L additive
M centre of mass  N island       O perturb object P contact split
Q camera        R reflection     S shadow         T transparent
U actuator      V tendon         W wireframe      X texture
Y range finder  Z light          and ' , / ; \\ ` as well
The letters here are the ones the tasks and the bundles bind. A key is bound
to what it does -- an axis of a command, a task's own control, a mode switch --
and never to a pad control: the keyboard is a path of its own beside the pad
(2026-09-29; until then it was a virtual pad read through the pad's mapping).
The jumper tasks: W A S D and the arrows walk, I K pitch, J L turn, H ; twist
(H left of J, ; right of L), U O roll, N M raise and lower, Esc lets go, and
in the claw modes Space closes the claw and Shift, Alt and Ctrl hold the arm
out. Q and O were the triggers and M the right stick's click until
2026-09-29; Shift + J L twisted and B let go until Control-agent 3.1 moved
them later that day, B to the right claw. Q is bound by nothing now.
So W also flips the scene to wireframe. That is accepted rather than unknown:
a keyboard laid out for the hands was worth more than a clean viewport, and
the flicker is visual only. A task that would rather not pay it binds the
keypad, which is still here and still free.
V, B, Space, 1 2 3 4 and Ctrl with them, on either row, switch the jumper
bundle's modes, each as its manifest entry's `keys` says: Space the jump, V
and B the claws, 1 2 3 4 the gestures, Ctrl + 1 2 3 4 the dances, and Ctrl on
its own leaves a dance or a gesture. They cost the viewer something too --
Space pauses it, V and B are tendons and perturb force -- and `play --app`
hands them to its controller down and up (`rl/mjrl/app_play.py`). What the
viewer does with Esc was not measured here.
The digits on the main row are the viewer's geom-group toggles, panels shown or
not. MEASURED (2026-09-28, keys sent to a viewer window, `opt.geomgroup` read
before and after): 1 to 4 each flip geom group 1 to 4 and the keypad's flip
nothing. On the jumper, whose appearance meshes are group 2 and collision
meshes group 1, 2 hides the robot the camera follows until pressed again and
1 draws its collision meshes over it. Accepted, as W's wireframe is; the
keypad digits are bound beside them and cost nothing.
The arrows cost the viewer less: left and right step a paused scene.
**MuJoCo's viewer reports a key's press and nothing else.** The callback is
handed a keycode and no action (`KeyCallbackType = Callable[[int], None]`), on
a press only: MuJoCo's GLFW adapter drops the auto-repeat and the release.
`mjrl.viewer.keys` puts a GLFW key callback of its own in front of the
viewer's and hands every reader both edges, so a key is held from its press to
its release, as in a browser, which reports both itself. Until 2026-09-29 the
release was inferred from repeats that never came, and every key let go 0.75 s
after its press.
Browser codes carry over unchanged -- `KeyW` is `KeyW` whatever the viewer
does -- so a web consumer pays nothing for this at all.

gestures.name: rise
gestures.fires: the tick it goes down, one-shot

gestures.name: fall
gestures.fires: the tick it comes back up, one-shot

gestures.name: hold
gestures.fires: every tick it is down -- a dead-man switch, not a mode

gestures.name: toggle
gestures.fires: down until pressed again -- the default for entering a mode

gestures.name: single
gestures.fires: one press and no second inside the click window; switches like `toggle`

gestures.name: double
gestures.fires: two presses, each inside the click window of the last; switches like `toggle`

gestures.name: triple
gestures.fires: three presses, each inside the click window of the last; switches like `toggle`

gestures.name: quadruple
gestures.fires: four presses, each inside the click window of the last; switches like `toggle`

gestures.name: quintuple
gestures.fires: five presses, each inside the click window of the last; switches like `toggle`

_gestures_note: A control may be bound more than once with different gestures: press to arm and release to go is one button, `rise` and `fall`, named twice. The five click gestures count presses of one control -- the same pad button or key, with the same modifier -- and a press counts when it comes within `click_window_ms` (`[fsm]` in the controller's config) of the one before. A count fires the binding for it the moment no longer count on that control is bound, and otherwise once the window has run out with no further press; so `single` fires at once where it is the only click on its control and waits out the window where a `double` shares it. A click switches a mode the way `toggle` does, and an `event` fires once. A control with a click gesture takes no `rise`, `fall`, `hold` or `toggle` -- every click would be one of those first. This note used to say there would be no double click, because counting needs a clock and a clock depends on how often a host ticks. The window is measured on the timestamps every host already hands the controller, not in ticks, so a host at 50 Hz and one at 1 kHz count the same presses the same way; the resolution is the host's rate, far inside any window a person can click to. No long press: nothing has asked for one.

absent.name: view
absent.why: The pad has this button and the service deliberately does not publish it. Binding it works on a bench through controller/xbox.py, which does report it, and does nothing at all on the robot.
